title: The Effect of Patient Cost Sharing on Utilization, Health, and Risk Protection
research_question: How does a substantial reduction in the share of medical costs that patients must pay out-of-pocket affect their use of health care services, their health outcomes, and their exposure to financial risk from medical expenditures, particularly among the elderly?
data_description: The study uses several Japanese administrative and survey datasets covering 1984–2008. The Patient Survey, a nationally representative repeated cross-section conducted every three years, provides patient-level outpatient records (one day in October) and inpatient discharge records (September), including exact dates of birth, admission, surgery, and discharge, along with diagnoses. Universe death records (1984–2008) include exact dates of birth and death, place, and ICD-9/10 cause of death. The Comprehensive Survey of Living Conditions (1986–2007) provides self-reported physical and mental health, employment, marital status, income, insurance coverage, and (in 2007) monthly out-of-pocket medical expenditures. The Survey of Medical Care Activities in Public Health Insurance provides individual-level monthly insurance claims used to compute out-of-pocket expenditures. The unit of observation is the individual patient, death, or survey respondent, typically aggregated to age in months for those aged 65–75.
institutional_context: Japan provides universal mandatory health insurance with unrestricted patient choice of providers, no gatekeeper or referral requirements, no deductibles, and a uniform national fee schedule that pays providers identically regardless of patient insurance type or age. Coinsurance rates and monthly stop-loss caps differ by age, with a sharp drop in patient cost sharing on the first day of the month after a person turns 70, when individuals become eligible for Elderly Health Insurance. Out-of-pocket cost sharing for both outpatient visits and inpatient admissions falls by roughly 60–80 percent at age 70; for inpatient care, monthly out-of-pocket expenditures for a 69-year-old can reach about 27 percent of average monthly income, while turning 70 reduces the counterfactual ratio to around 8.6 percent. Crucially, turning 70 in Japan does not coincide with changes in employment, pension receipt, or insurance coverage status, isolating the change in benefit generosity.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Increased patient cost sharing leads to a reduction in healthcare utilization without significant adverse effects on health outcomes.
